headline: Reagan sworn in for a second term
text: Ronald Reagan began his second term as US president on 20 January, with George H. W. Bush again as vice president. The budget deficit and the dollar are the big questions for the markets.

headline: The dollar is a third higher than in 1980
text: Since 1980 the US dollar has gained about 50% against the Japanese yen, the German mark, the French franc and the British pound. That makes imports cheap for Americans and American exports dear abroad.

headline: Daimler-Benz delivers its new mid-size Mercedes
text: Customers began receiving the new Mercedes-Benz W124 range in January: petrol models from the 200 and 230E up to the six-cylinder 260E and 300E, plus three diesels. It replaces the W123 range.

headline: Nestle now owns Carnation, bought for 3 billion dollars
text: The Swiss food group Nestle has bought the American company Carnation for $3 billion. Carnation brings the evaporated milk brand, Coffee-Mate creamer and Friskies pet food into Nestle. Sources differ on whether the deal dates from 1984 or 1985.

headline: Saudi Arabia cuts its oil price to 28 dollars a barrel
text: Saudi Arabia cut the price of its light crude by one dollar to $28 a barrel in January, and nine OPEC members narrowed the price gap between light and heavy crude. Cheaper oil is welcome for drivers and less welcome for oil companies like Exxon.

headline: Pop stars record "We Are the World" for Ethiopia
text: On 28 January American pop stars recorded the charity song "We Are the World" as USA for Africa. The money raised is meant to fight the famine in Ethiopia.

headline: Gibraltar border reopens after 16 years
text: On 4 February the border between Gibraltar and Spain opened again after 16 years. Families and shoppers on both sides can cross once more.

headline: Israel starts pulling troops out of Lebanon
text: On 16 February Israel began withdrawing its troops from Lebanon. The same month Hezbollah, a militant group based in Lebanon, declared its ideology publicly.

headline: A year after launch, the Macintosh is struggling
text: Apple's Macintosh went on sale in January 1984 at $2,495, but sales fell sharply in the second half of 1984. Buyers complain that it has only 128 KB of memory and too little software. Apple needs a second act.

headline: First artificial heart patient goes home
text: William Schroeder, who received an artificial heart, was discharged from hospital on 19 February, the first such patient to leave.

headline: Gorbachev takes over the Soviet Union
text: Mikhail Gorbachev, 54, was chosen on 11 March as general secretary of the Soviet Communist Party after Konstantin Chernenko died. The West is trying to work out what the new man wants.

headline: Capital Cities buys ABC for 3.5 billion dollars
text: On 18 March the small broadcaster Capital Cities announced it will buy the ABC television network for $3.5 billion, the biggest merger outside the oil industry so far. ABC is about four times bigger than the buyer. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway helps finance the deal and is to get about a quarter of the combined company.

headline: Apple launches the LaserWriter printer
text: In March Apple introduced the LaserWriter, a laser printer that works with the Macintosh. Together with page-layout software it lets anyone design and print a newsletter or brochure at a desk, which people now call desktop publishing.

headline: "Amadeus" wins the Oscar for best picture
text: The film Amadeus won Best Picture at the Academy Awards on 25 March.

headline: Coca-Cola changes its recipe: "New Coke" launches
text: On 23 April Coca-Cola replaced its original formula with a new one, New Coke. The company says the new drink beat both old Coke and Pepsi in taste tests, but its customer hotline is now getting more than 1,500 calls a day, up from about 400, and many callers are angry.

headline: Japan privatises its phone and tobacco monopolies
text: On 1 April Japan turned its state telephone company and its state tobacco company into private corporations.

headline: Rupert Murdoch buys half of Twentieth Century Fox
text: The Australian publisher Rupert Murdoch bought 50% of the parent company of the Hollywood studio Twentieth Century Fox for $250 million.

headline: South Africa ends its ban on mixed marriages
text: On 15 April South Africa ended its ban on marriage between people of different races.

headline: Industrial Bank of Japan, banker to Japan's big industry, is now available
text: The Industrial Bank of Japan, founded in 1902 as a state-backed bank, joins the game. It is a long-term credit bank: since 1952 it lends mostly for many years to big industry, funding itself by issuing bonds called debentures to other financial institutions. It has no corporate family of its own, is second banker to all the big ones, and holds shares in many clients.

headline: The Dow closes above 1,300 for the first time
text: On 20 May the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 1,304.88, its first close above 1,300. The index of 30 big US companies has been climbing in a bull market that began in 1982.

headline: Scientists report a hole in the ozone layer
text: On 16 May the British Antarctic Survey announced that the ozone layer above Antarctica, which shields life from the sun's ultraviolet light, has a hole in it.

headline: Two football disasters in three weeks
text: A fire at the Bradford City stadium killed 56 people on 11 May. On 29 May, 39 people died at the Heysel Stadium in Brussels before the European Cup final.

headline: Hijackers seize TWA flight 847
text: Hezbollah hijackers took over TWA flight 847 on 14 June and killed one passenger.

headline: Air India jumbo jet bombed, 329 dead
text: Air India flight 182 was bombed on 23 June and all 329 people on board were killed.

headline: OPEC output falls to a 20-year low
text: OPEC's oil output fell in June to 13.7 million barrels a day, the lowest in 20 years. The group is holding oil back to protect the price, which is good for the price but costs its members sales.

headline: Route 66 is officially retired
text: The American road made famous by songs and films, U.S. Route 66, was officially decommissioned on 26 June.

headline: Coca-Cola brings the old formula back after 79 days
text: On 11 July Coca-Cola announced the original recipe will return as Coca-Cola Classic. The company had received over 40,000 angry calls and letters since 23 April, and 31,600 more calls came in the two days after the announcement. Sales were up 8% on the year before, so it was not the money but the fuss.

headline: Live Aid: two stadiums, 1.9 billion viewers
text: On 13 July concerts at Wembley in London and in Philadelphia, organised by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure, were watched by an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries. Between 40 and 50 million pounds were reported raised for famine relief in Ethiopia.

headline: "Back to the Future" hits the cinemas
text: Back to the Future opened in US cinemas on 3 July. It is one of the many youth-oriented science-fiction comedies and fantasy films crowding the cinemas this year.

headline: Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior bombed and sunk
text: On 10 July the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was bombed and sunk in a New Zealand harbour. French agents are blamed.

headline: Buffett closes the last Berkshire textile mill
text: Warren Buffett decided in August to close Berkshire Hathaway's last textile factory in New Bedford, laying off the remaining 400 or so workers. Berkshire began as a cloth maker and has now left that business entirely.

headline: Two air disasters in two weeks
text: Delta flight 191 crashed near Dallas on 2 August and killed 137 people. On 12 August Japan Air Lines flight 123 crashed in Japan and killed 520, the deadliest crash of a single aircraft ever.

headline: Saudi Arabia links its oil price to the spot market
text: In August Saudi Arabia tied its crude price to the spot market, where oil is sold for immediate delivery, and its output begins to rise from 2 million barrels a day. Until now the kingdom held oil back to protect the price. Oil companies and oilfield firms such as Schlumberger are watching.

headline: Five nations agree to push the dollar down
text: On 22 September the finance ministers of the US, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain agreed at the Plaza Hotel in New York that the dollar should fall. The dollar dropped 4% the following Monday. Japan's exporters, whose goods get dearer, are the most exposed.

headline: Philip Morris to buy General Foods for 5.8 billion dollars
text: The cigarette maker Philip Morris announced on 28 September that it will buy General Foods for about $5.8 billion, the largest takeover outside the oil industry so far. A tobacco company is moving into food.

headline: Steve Jobs leaves Apple
text: On 17 September Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, handed in his resignation. He lost a power struggle with chief executive John Sculley, whose May reorganisation would have taken the Macintosh group away from him, and the board backed Sculley.

headline: Super Mario Bros. is released in Japan
text: Nintendo released Super Mario Bros. on 13 September for its Famicom console, which has been selling in Japan since 1983.

headline: Sony shows Handycam, a camera and recorder in one
text: Sony's Handycam, announced in September, records on small Video8 cassettes, which allows a camcorder small enough to hold in one hand, instead of the bigger shoulder-mounted cameras.

headline: BMW shows its M3 racing special in Frankfurt
text: BMW presented the M3 at the Frankfurt Motor Show. It is a road car built so that it can race in touring-car championships, which require 5,000 to be built, and it has a high-revving four-cylinder engine of about 200 horsepower.

headline: Earthquake devastates Mexico City
text: An earthquake of magnitude 8.0 hit Mexico City on 19 September. Estimates of the dead range from 5,000 to 45,000.

headline: Northwest orders ten of Boeing's new 747-400
text: On 22 October Northwest Airlines ordered ten 747-400s, which launched the new version of Boeing's jumbo jet. It has longer wings with winglets at the tips, a cockpit run by two pilots instead of three, and room for about 416 passengers.

headline: Intel introduces the 80386, a 32-bit chip
text: In October Intel introduced the 80386, its first processor that handles data 32 bits at a time and can address up to 4 gigabytes of memory. Intel will make it in its own factories in California, Oregon and Arizona and will not license it to rivals.

headline: Nintendo's console goes on sale in New York
text: On 18 October the Nintendo Entertainment System appeared in a test market in New York City. The Deluxe Set costs $179.99 and includes a light gun, a toy robot and two games, and Super Mario Bros. is the key title.

headline: The first Blockbuster video store opens in Dallas
text: The first Blockbuster Video store opened in Dallas, Texas, on 19 October.

headline: McDonald's opens its first restaurant in Mexico
text: On 29 October the first McDonald's in Mexico opened in Pedregal, Mexico City, run by a local partner, Saul Kahan.

headline: Hijackers seize the cruise ship Achille Lauro
text: On 7 October hijackers took over the Italian cruise ship Achille Lauro and killed Leon Klinghoffer, an American passenger.

headline: Reagan and Gorbachev meet for the first time
text: US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva on 19 November. It is their first meeting, and the topic is nuclear weapons.

headline: The Dow climbs above 1,400
text: On 6 November the Dow Jones index closed at 1,403.44, its first close above 1,400. It first closed above 1,300 less than six months ago.

headline: Microsoft releases Windows 1.0
text: On 20 November Microsoft, the maker of the MS-DOS software that runs IBM PCs, released Windows 1.0, a graphical layer that runs on top of DOS.

headline: Volcano buries the Colombian town of Armero
text: Colombia's Nevado del Ruiz volcano erupted on 13 November, and about 23,000 people died in the town of Armero.

headline: Kasparov becomes world chess champion at 22
text: Garry Kasparov beat Anatoly Karpov on 9 November, becoming the youngest world chess champion at age 22.

headline: General Electric agrees to buy RCA and NBC for 6.3 billion dollars
text: In December General Electric announced it will buy RCA for $6.28 billion, mostly to own the NBC television network. It is the biggest takeover outside the oil industry, topping Capital Cities' purchase of ABC from March. GE has been led by Jack Welch since 1981.

headline: Congress sets a path to a balanced budget
text: President Reagan signed the Gramm-Rudman-Hollings law on 12 December. It sets lower deficit targets each year and orders automatic spending cuts if Congress misses them. The deficit is the biggest in dollar terms in US history, $212 billion in 1985.

headline: The Dow ends the year at 1,546.67, up 28%
text: The Dow closed above 1,500 for the first time on 11 December (1,511.70) and ended 1985 at 1,546.67, up 27.66% on the year.

headline: OPEC pumps 18 million barrels a day as a price war starts
text: OPEC's output hit 18 million barrels a day in December, up from 13.7 million in June. With too much oil around, a price war is starting between producers who want to protect their share of the market.

headline: Wal-Mart now has 882 stores
text: By the end of 1985 Wal-Mart ran 882 stores with sales of $8.4 billion and 104,000 employees. It has opened its first stores in Virginia, Wisconsin and Colorado in the last two years.

headline: Siemens buys out its American partner Allis-Chalmers
text: During 1985 Siemens bought the stake of Allis-Chalmers in Siemens-Allis, the joint company formed in 1978 that supplies electrical control equipment in the US.
